video_title: How Lassie Is Automating Healthcare Administration
gist: Lassie's founders (Stein, ex-Robin Hood; Frederick, ex-Superhuman) and an a16z partner (Alex) argue that AI's real TAM is not software budgets but labor budgets: Lassie sells a fully autonomous billing/payments agent to US dental practices where 160,000 offices each spend ~$200k/year on admin and literally cannot hire staff. The conversation details how they bootstrapped automation by doing the billing work by hand in offices, why 98% autonomy with no human in the loop is the product requirement, why verticals with no incumbent software vendor are structurally safer than 'Workday but AI', and how a federal mandate forcing insurers to offer direct deposit (70% of these businesses are still paid on paper) is the regulatory unlock that makes the work automatable at all.

themes.theme: Software doing labor, not storing data

insights.claim: Alex frames the entire history of software as digitizing filing cabinets — Sabre for airline reservations, PeopleSoft for HR, LexisNexis for legal, QuickBooks and NetSuite for accounting — which moved storage but left humans doing the actual work.
insights.speaker: Alex
insights.so_what: If storage-era SaaS never removed headcount, the incremental value of AI that actually executes the work is a step-change, not a multiple of existing software spend.
insights.quote: software just kind of took things that were stored in paper format and then they made them available first on prem via green screen computers but people still had to do the work

insights.claim: Alex claims software historically did not make organizations more efficient: HR departments employed roughly the same number of people per company size in 1950 as in 2000, with filing-cabinet guards simply replaced by IT departments and a CISO.
insights.speaker: Alex
insights.so_what: A deflationary read on legacy SaaS ROI; supports rotating exposure from workflow tools toward vendors billing against labor line items.
insights.quote: the same number of people worked in HR for the exact same size company in like 1950 as probably 2000

insights.claim: Alex's core thesis is that the volume of work performed on stored information is orders of magnitude larger than the market for storing that information, so AI that edits the filing cabinet rather than just holding it addresses a vastly bigger market.
insights.speaker: Alex
insights.so_what: Sizes the AI opportunity off services and payroll spend rather than the ~$1T software market, justifying far higher revenue ceilings per vertical.
insights.quote: So it just turns out that the work is orders of magnitude bigger than the storage of information that the work is done on.

insights.claim: Alex uses Toast to argue fintech bundling was the prior TAM expansion: restaurant software was technically possible on MS-DOS in 1985 but no restaurant would pay $100,000 for it, whereas a ~2% payments take rate lets you collect that amount invisibly.
insights.speaker: Alex
insights.so_what: The same monetization logic now applies to labor: charging out of the payroll budget is the next bundling wave after payments attach.
insights.quote: nobody would pay $100,000 for that. But if you bundle in payment processing, you're effectively charging $100,000 for that, right? Because maybe you get a 2% vig.

insights.claim: Alex argues selling labor beats selling software because the vendor can charge for work done cheaper and better than humans — but says even that framing undersells it, since in many cases no human is available at any price.
insights.speaker: Alex
insights.so_what: Demand for AI labor in SMB services is not a cost-substitution trade; it's filling unfillable roles, which supports pricing power and low churn.
insights.quote: It's not like, oh, AI is going to take the jobs. In many cases, you can't find somebody.

insights.claim: Alex models unmet SMB demand as a market failure — everything to the right of the supply-demand equilibrium — where a service everyone would pay a dollar for costs $100 to produce, and only near-zero-cost AI labor clears it.
insights.speaker: Alex
insights.so_what: A screening heuristic: hunt for roles that are economically rational to want but irrational to hire, since those convert instantly to AI seats.
insights.quote: imagine that there is something that every human on earth would pay a dollar for but the cost of manufacturing that thing is $100. You just have a market failure

insights.claim: Alex says the public markets are pricing software as dead and AI as the winner, while VCs treat AI as software — and that pure-play software companies not shipping AI features are 'smoking crack' because customers are demanding them.
insights.speaker: Alex
insights.so_what: Flags a market dislocation: the software/AI dichotomy in public multiples may be false, creating both value traps and mispriced incumbents.
insights.quote: if you look at the public markets the public markets are saying in many cases like oh you're a software company software is dead, software socks, software is zero. Oh, you're an AI. It's the opposite of what VCs are saying.

themes.theme: The Betty shortage: SMB admin as the wedge

insights.claim: Lassie was founded after Stein watched his own dentist, Dr. Quan, the number-one-rated doctor on Yelp, spend 200 hours a month on paperwork and submit insurance claims by hand because he could not hire billing staff.
insights.speaker: Stein
insights.so_what: The founding observation quantifies the labor pool being displaced: 200 hours/month per practice is the revenue pool an agent can attack.
insights.quote: the number one rated doctor on Yelp spending 200 hours a month on paperwork and busy work

insights.claim: Stein cites roughly 160,000 dental practices in the US each spending about $200,000 a year on administrative costs, which he converts into a ~$1 billion recurring-revenue market for dental alone.
insights.speaker: Stein
insights.so_what: A concrete bottom-up TAM for vertical SMB AI; the same arithmetic can be applied to other practitioner verticals.
insights.quote: there about like 160,000 dental practices in the US alone and like they spend roughly $200,000 a year on like administrative costs

insights.claim: Lassie is already charging five figures per year for a first agent that performs only about 30 hours of labor a month against roughly 200 hours of available work, implying substantial headroom to expand contract value per practice.
insights.speaker: Stein
insights.so_what: Land-and-expand economics are explicit: ~15% of the addressable labor at a five-figure ACV suggests multi-fold net revenue retention potential.
insights.quote: we are already charging five figures for kind of like this first agent that only does 30 hours uh of labor a month and there's 200 hours of labors to be done for Dr. Loop

insights.claim: Alex recounts that his childhood dentist Dr. Sloop retired specifically because he lost the woman who did his books and could not replace her, and told Alex he would not have retired if Lassie had existed.
insights.speaker: Alex
insights.so_what: Admin burden is causing practitioner supply to exit the market — AI admin tools may increase practitioner supply, not just cut cost.
insights.quote: And he said that if this had been around, he wouldn't have retired.

insights.claim: Stein says Lassie encounters doctors with Harvard degrees personally doing billing until midnight, and that these owners are close to quitting the parts of the job they hate — which makes them adopt AI fast rather than skeptically.
insights.speaker: Stein
insights.so_what: Contradicts the assumed SMB AI-skepticism barrier; the binding constraint is reach, not persuasion.
insights.quote: these people are in real pain and they are to Alex's point about to quit or just like they hate their job

insights.claim: Alex characterizes the competitive incumbent in dental administration not as a software vendor but as departed staff — 'the incumbent was named Betty and she quit two weeks ago' — or an offshore billing agency.
insights.speaker: Alex
insights.so_what: Competitive analysis for AI-labor companies should benchmark against wage rates and outsourcing agencies, not SaaS seat prices.
insights.quote: Well, the incumbent was named Betty and she quit two weeks ago. That's the incumbent.

insights.claim: Stein describes the daily grind Lassie replaces as updating roughly 200 ledgers a week, visiting insurance portals, updating a system of record and checking the bank account 200 times a week — and says cutting that to a handful saves 10 to 20 hours.
insights.speaker: Stein
insights.so_what: Quantifies the value delivered per customer, anchoring both pricing and the ROI story used in word-of-mouth sales.
insights.quote: you have like to update 200 ledgers a week because that's how much patience you see and then you have to like go to an insurance portal update like a system of record check against the bank account 200 times a week

themes.theme: Building agents with no human in the loop

insights.claim: Frederick decomposes job automation into three layers — context (historical data, patient records), tools to do the work, and intelligence — and says Lassie built context and tools from 2020 when models were weak, then swapped in better models as an unearned tailwind.
insights.speaker: Frederick
insights.so_what: A durable build order for vertical AI: proprietary context and write-access tooling compound while the intelligence layer commoditizes.
insights.quote: we started building uh building the context layer and building the tools and it and it's just that the intelligence layer wasn't that intelligent

insights.claim: Lassie bootstrapped automation by having its founders act as the humans in the loop — literally doing billing inside offices — and then automating away their own work, which Frederick says was necessary to build a product that works.
insights.speaker: Frederick
insights.so_what: A repeatable playbook (and a diligence question) for services-to-software AI companies: did the team do the job before encoding it?
insights.quote: Initially we were actually the humans in the loop. We kind of automated away our own problems.

insights.claim: Frederick sets an internal bar of roughly 95%+ automation before selling a product, deliberately refusing to wait for 100% and instead moving to the next job once one is taken over, optimizing share of the whole business automated rather than per-product perfection.
insights.speaker: Frederick
insights.so_what: Defines a shippable-autonomy threshold for agent products and explains why breadth beats depth in expanding ACV.
insights.quote: we want to get to like a sufficient level of automation across any product to uh before we sell it. So you know for us I think that's like 95 plus say but not necessarily 100

insights.claim: Stein argues SMB AI cannot use the human-in-the-loop pattern most AI companies rely on, because there is no staffer left to review output — forcing an agent that errs on the side of correctness and takes years longer to build.
insights.speaker: Stein
insights.so_what: Raises the technical bar (and the moat) for SMB agents relative to enterprise copilots that can lean on reviewers.
insights.quote: we needed to build an agent. That's why it took us years that like airs on the side of correctness

insights.claim: Frederick says the structural difference between SMB and enterprise software is that in SMBs there is nobody available to use the tool at all, so tool-shaped products fail regardless of quality.
insights.speaker: Frederick
insights.so_what: Explains why SMB SaaS historically underperformed and why outcome-delivery pricing is the only viable SMB AI model.
insights.quote: a huge difference uh between SMBs in general and and enterprises is that in SMBs there's nobody to to use the tools

insights.claim: Lassie says thousands of staffers across its customer base feed corrections back into the agent, and Stein claims about 98% of the work is handled by the first agent with a sliver left for humans.
insights.speaker: Stein
insights.so_what: A distributed human-feedback loop across many small customers is a data moat unavailable to single-enterprise deployments.
insights.quote: it's fine if it does in this case for the first agent 98% of the work and then there's a sliver left

insights.claim: Stein says the defensibility comes from stitching read-and-write integrations across systems and building an ontology so every party agrees on what an insurance claim or patient payment means, since each system defines them differently.
insights.speaker: Stein
insights.so_what: The moat in vertical AI is data-model and integration work, not model access — hard to replicate with a coding agent.
insights.quote: you need to build an ontology to make sure that everybody in this whole ecosystem is on the same page about an insurance claim and the patient payment because all these different systems have like a slightly different definition of that

themes.theme: Moats when the category has no software incumbent

insights.claim: Alex restates his rule that the battle between startup and incumbent comes down to whether the startup gets distribution before the incumbent gets the innovation, and warns that AI shortens the incumbent's time to innovation.
insights.speaker: Alex
insights.so_what: Raises the bar for feature-shaped AI startups sitting on top of an existing platform; speed of distribution is the only defense.
insights.quote: the battle between every startup and incumbent comes down to whether the startup gets the distribution before the incumbent gets the innovation

insights.claim: Alex argues AI erodes a key reason incumbents fail to copy startups — that big companies hire bad engineers and carry heavy process — because AI turns a bad engineer into a decent one.
insights.speaker: Alex
insights.so_what: Implies shorter windows for AI feature startups and a re-rating of incumbents' ability to defend, particularly in categories they already own.
insights.quote: one of the reasons is they hire very bad engineers and they have lots of process, but now AI kind of makes a bad engineer into like a pretty good engineer, you know, kind of

insights.claim: Alex's 'TiVo problem' framework says companies that build a feature on someone else's pipe face only bad outcomes: a control discount from the one buyer who can acquire you, a worse copy years later, or a licensing deal where the distributor takes the economics.
insights.speaker: Alex
insights.so_what: A diligence filter: verify a startup owns the customer relationship or pipe, not just the differentiated feature.
insights.quote: you you have what what I call a control discount versus a control premium

insights.claim: Alex says his TrialPay-era lesson was that startups should build the boring pipe first — he realized four years in he should have built Stripe, because owning commodity payment processing wins the customer chronologically and lets you add the lucrative layer on top.
insights.speaker: Alex
insights.so_what: Supports backing 'boring infrastructure first' AI companies over feature-led ones, since ownership of the pipe gates the profitable products.
insights.quote: wow we should we should do boring payment processing which is a commodity business because if we do that then we own the customer

insights.claim: Alex uses X1 (Outlook search, VC-funded, eventually sold to Yahoo for little) as the cautionary case of building an obviously great feature in a category the platform owner would inevitably absorb.
insights.speaker: Alex
insights.so_what: Historical analog for today's AI wrappers built on top of dominant productivity suites.

insights.claim: Alex's key AI-era amendment is that many AI-does-the-work categories are non-categories with no software incumbent at all, because the only prior solution was human labor — which removes the platform-absorption risk entirely.
insights.speaker: Alex
insights.so_what: The cleanest screen for AI investing: prefer verticals where labor, not software, is the incumbent; be wary of 'Workday but AI'.
insights.quote: there are a lot of categories where there never was an incumbent software company because the only job to be done was like actual human labor

themes.theme: Reaching Main Street: SMB go-to-market and onboarding

insights.claim: Alex's framing that AI is overhyped in Silicon Valley but underhyped in Iowa positions the distribution of AI to non-technical mainstream businesses, not model capability, as the binding constraint on value creation.
insights.speaker: Alex
insights.so_what: Directs capital toward last-mile distribution and onboarding rather than another model or dev-tool layer.
insights.quote: AI is overhyped in Silicon Valley but underhyped in Iowa

insights.claim: Stein contrasts the current AI cutting edge — a few steak dinners and a contract producing $10 million of booked ARR from enterprises — with Lassie's need to find thousands to hundreds of thousands of small businesses, requiring a wholly different playbook.
insights.speaker: Stein
insights.so_what: SMB AI revenue will look slower and more capital-intensive early but with far less concentration risk than enterprise land-grabs.
insights.quote: you have these models good enough and apply them in enterprises and you do like a few stake dinners and then you sign a contract and then you have like 10 million in AR booked, right?

insights.claim: Stein says standard B2B prospecting stacks fail for this customer because Dr. Sloop is not in Clay or Apollo databases and often not on LinkedIn, forcing Lassie to map practices, owners, systems in use and intent signals such as job postings on Indeed.
insights.speaker: Stein
insights.so_what: A proprietary SMB data and outbound layer is itself a moat; incumbent GTM tooling does not reach this buyer.
insights.quote: We can't really do that because Dr. Sloop is not in that database. He's often not on LinkedIn.

insights.claim: Stein says Lassie's consumer backgrounds at Robin Hood and Superhuman set a 48-hour window to deliver core product value, and that busy non-technical doctors will drop the product within months if it does not simply work once plugged in.
insights.speaker: Stein
insights.so_what: Consumer-grade activation metrics, not enterprise implementation cycles, are the right operating KPIs for SMB AI.

insights.claim: Lassie's onboarding is nearly self-serve: the doctor goes through a Stripe-like checkout or Replit-like flow linking the practice bank account, the system of record and the insurance portals, with configuration handled under the hood — modeled on how Robin Hood removed humans from brokerage account opening.
insights.speaker: Stein
insights.so_what: Automated onboarding is the unit-economics lever that decides whether SMB AI scales or requires a field-services army.
insights.quote: the onboarding needs to be as simple as onboarding on Coinbase

insights.claim: Frederick says Lassie is strict about ICP because onboarding a practice whose work it cannot substantially automate is more painful than a mis-sold traditional product — the company either fails on its automation promise or has to offboard the customer.
insights.speaker: Frederick
insights.so_what: Outcome-based AI pricing makes customer selection an underwriting decision; loose qualification shows up later as churn.
insights.quote: focusing on uh the right ICP and being really strict about who you onboard uh to basically guarantee that uh they're going to have a great experience

insights.claim: Stein says a federal mandate requiring the industry to stop paper checks and offer direct deposit to doctors — plus digital itemized invoice formats — is the regulatory inflection that makes this work automatable at all.
insights.speaker: Stein
insights.so_what: The automation opportunity is timing-dependent on a regulatory forcing function; similar mandates elsewhere would flag the next vertical.
insights.quote: And then the federal government stepped in and they said this has to stop, right? You cannot do paper checks anymore for much longer.

insights.claim: Stein estimates around 70% of these small businesses are still paid on paper and says the industry is going through a massive digitization revolution driven by that federal inflection point.
insights.speaker: Stein
insights.so_what: A quantified conversion runway; every practice flipped to digital deposits is a newly automatable account.
insights.quote: I think the stats are 70% are still paid uh on paper and it's going through this massive like digitization revolution right now because federal inflection point that's regulatory

insights.claim: Stein says even perfect models five years ago could not have done this job because the file cabinet was literally physical — he personally opened envelopes from the mailman and deposited $100,000 of paper checks with itemized invoices attached for Dr. Quan.
insights.speaker: Stein
insights.so_what: Model capability is not sufficient for vertical automation; data availability in digital form is the gating input to watch.
insights.quote: and I kid you not, I open all these envelopes, deposit $100,000, like cash uh, in the bank account of the doctor

insights.claim: Stein says the reason practices have not flipped to digital payments themselves is a 50-hour switching cost across Cigna, Delta and other carriers plus the problem that bank-account access would expose data staff should not see — so Lassie productized the conversion for them.
insights.speaker: Stein
insights.so_what: The conversion engine is a distinct, defensible product layer beneath the agent, and a barrier that a pure model-wrapper cannot replicate.
insights.quote: Dr. loop needs to also then spend 50 hours figuring out with Sigma and Delta and all the other insurance companies, how do I flip the switch?

insights.claim: Frederick argues payments stayed on paper partly because staff prefer working off physical sheets — digitizing without tools just yields a PDF that is harder to use — so there was no incentive to digitize until agents could act on the data.
insights.speaker: Frederick
insights.so_what: Explains why digitization stalled for decades and why AI changes the incentive; a pattern to look for in other paper-bound industries.
insights.quote: Part of the reason that uh all of these payments are still on paper is that the staff basically prefers doing the work by hand on paper.

themes.theme: Insurance dynamics and the marginal cost of arguing

insights.claim: Alex raises the question of what happens to insurance payments and collections when the marginal cost of arguing goes to zero and both sides can dispute in perpetuity using AI.
insights.speaker: Alex
insights.so_what: An unpriced second-order risk for insurers, claims processors and collections businesses if adjudication costs rise on both sides.
insights.quote: how the world changes when the marginal cost of arguing goes to zero

insights.claim: Alex claims his health insurer Cigna sends only paper checks with no online enrollment as intentional friction, betting recipients lose or fail to deposit them, mirroring the deny-deny-deny posture of insurance broadly.
insights.speaker: Alex
insights.so_what: Float and breakage from friction is a real income stream for carriers that agentic automation could compress.
insights.quote: Sigma, who I have for my health insurance, will only send paper checks. I was like, "Oh, I must have missed the whole like online enrollment." Nope. Nope. They don't have one.

insights.claim: Stein counters that dental billing is well-regulated and rule-based — a carrier document specifies exactly which X-ray and narrative justify covering a crown — which is precisely why agents outperform humans who cannot remember 50 to 100 common billing codes.
insights.speaker: Stein
insights.so_what: Codified-rule domains with poor human compliance are the highest-yield targets for agents; expect claim approval rates to rise as a measurable outcome.
insights.quote: take dentistry there like 50 60 maybe 100 common billing codes

insights.claim: Stein argues carriers have a countervailing incentive to keep good dentists in network and paid, because employers shopping plans annually will switch carriers if covered dentists in the area are poor — limiting how adversarial the payer relationship becomes.
insights.speaker: Stein
insights.so_what: Tempers the assumption that payer automation is purely adversarial; carriers may cooperate with agentic billing that reduces network friction.

themes.theme: Master plan, model limits and building a 2026 company

insights.claim: Lassie's stated end goal is that every small business runs itself, with a business agent interfacing with a consumer's personal agent and with agents at insurance companies and other counterparties.
insights.speaker: Stein
insights.so_what: Agent-to-agent commerce as the terminal state implies infrastructure needs — identity, authorization, settlement — as an investable adjacency.
insights.quote: every small business should run itself, right? And the busy work is done by uh agents

insights.claim: Frederick says frontier models trained on vast data still do not know how to do this work because the workflows are not encoded anywhere — the knowledge sits in office managers' heads and is not accessible on the internet, so Lassie collects SOPs and infers workflows from customers' historical ERP data.
insights.speaker: Frederick
insights.so_what: Tacit-workflow data is the scarce input in vertical AI; companies with write access to historical operational data hold the real advantage over model access.
insights.quote: The models are trained on so much data and they're so large and yet they actually don't really know how to do any of this work.

insights.claim: Frederick names slow learning as the outstanding technical gap and says he is personally excited about smaller models that learn faster on less data, while acknowledging that might not benefit Lassie specifically.
insights.speaker: Frederick
insights.so_what: A practitioner's signal that sample-efficient small models, not bigger frontier models, are the next unlock for vertical automation.
insights.quote: I'm I'm personally kind of excited about uh smaller models that uh, you know, learn faster and can learn on less data

insights.claim: Frederick says product building has shifted from shipping functionality to eliminating work: instead of building the ability to send a statement, the target is that the office spends zero further time on patient billing including the follow-up phone calls where the time actually goes.
insights.speaker: Frederick
insights.so_what: Reframes product scoping around time-and-motion analysis of where labor hours actually go, usually customer communication rather than transactions.
insights.quote: once we deliver patient billing the office should not have to spend any more time on patient billing which is super different to giving them a tool that they then need to use

insights.claim: Stein's contrarian hiring take is that nothing has changed on talent quality — you still need top-five-percentile engineers or sellers with steep slope — but Lassie now interviews specifically for how AI-pilled a candidate is across every function including finance.
insights.speaker: Stein
insights.so_what: An operating template for 2026 org design: same talent bar, new screen for AI-native working assumptions in non-engineering roles.
insights.quote: You still need people with steep slope um that like are very ambitious and and driven uh and have skills that are just like top five percentile either in engineering or in selling

insights.claim: Stein says the goal is a 2026-version organization that ships twice as much as others and moves four times as fast, and calls the output-per-person multiple of four to five the big open experiment of company building right now.
insights.speaker: Stein
insights.so_what: A falsifiable productivity claim to test against headcount and revenue disclosures at AI-native startups.
insights.quote: we want to build a 2026 version of a of a of a big organization right uh where like we ship twice as much than others. We move like four times as like fast

insights.claim: Alex poses the paradox that if AI makes small businesses far easier to start and run, competition could erode SMB margins — since the accumulation of people needed to deliver the service was itself the small business's moat.
insights.speaker: Alex
insights.so_what: A downside scenario for the AI-for-SMB thesis: commoditized service supply could compress the very margins that fund the software.
insights.quote: it could actually work out where like small businesses it's much easier to start one and run one but then actually paradoxically it's much harder to be one

insights.claim: Stein rebuts the margin-erosion risk by arguing demand is not capped but supply-constrained — there is roughly twice as much dental and plumbing demand as can be supplied — so the outcome could be half a million dentists or the same dentists seeing twice as many patients.
insights.speaker: Stein
insights.so_what: If correct, AI expands service-sector volume rather than compressing price, which is bullish for SMB-serving vendors and for healthcare access volumes.
insights.quote: this assumes there's a cap on kind of like demand and if you just look at the dental practice, but the same applies to try to find a good plumber
